messages.author: c8fe4075ec631c03
messages.subject: Performance, parallelism
parts:
Hi Winston,

  I have now deployed my application internally at my company, and after the announcement it all went SLOW.

  Am I right in thinking that the shiny server is fundamentally serial and blocking across multiple users?

  Is there any way to change this - for instance fork a new R instance (ala library(parallel)) to prevent blocking?

-Alex

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: Performance, parallelism
parts:
Shiny Server is not fundamentally serial but R is. Right now Shiny Server directs all users for a given app to the same R process, which is why all users end up being serial.

There are two ways to address this (that can be used in combination).

1) Run multiple Shiny Server processes and/or machines and put them behind a load balancer. For multiple Shiny Server processes per machine, you'd need to have a config file per Shiny Server process and have each process listening on a different port.
2) Configure Shiny Server to launch multiple processes for a given app. This isn't currently possible but is on the plan for later this year.

How urgent is the bottleneck for you right now? Is the app unusable for you as deployed right now, or was it just right after your announcement?

Since it's my first post on this group I would like to start with saying "Hi" to everybody and "Thank you" the dev team for great work on Shiny.

I have similar problem with application I'm developing and running on Shiny Server. 
In the first attempt I used the cluster module from Node.js as shown here: http://nodejs.org/api/cluster.html

I modified the https://github.com/rstudio/shiny-server/blob/master/lib/main.js file in the following way:

//[modules, variables, etc.]
if (cluster.isMaster) {
  for (var i = 0; i < numCPUs; i++) {
    cluster.fork();
  }
  cluster.on('exit', function(worker, code, signal) {
    console.log('worker ' + worker.process.pid + ' died');
  });
} else {
   //[original main.js code]
}
The server started correctly, node process was spawned 4 times (4 cores VM); while trying to access the apps the R processes started (one R process per each node process), but no response was send to the browser. It seems to me that there is some problem with sockjs not being able to talk to browser from node.js child process. Maybe you can help with that.

Now I am trying to achieve the parallelization from within R - I am using the multicore::parallel function to fork most computationally expensive functions to other process(es) and periodically run multicore::collect from main process to determine if computation is done. So far looks simple and promising, I'll share the results when I finish the implementation.

messages.subject: Re: Performance, parallelism
parts:
Hmm, the problem I currently have is actually that our local NIS server cluster is poorly performing.

It seems that unlike most server applications, R makes a lot of calls onto NIS, via getpwuid.

This function is called by do_fileinfo  - presumably invoked by file.info.

For some reason, file.info always retrieves (via an internal function) the uid translated into the username - even if it has asked the same question MANY times before.

part of this problem is that I'm using a network user, but my company policies make this (if not unavoidable) very hard to avoid.

As you guys are R core - can you suggest any way to cause caching of UID->username lookup?

I'm considering building an LD_PRELOAD'ed cache.

-Alex

parts:
okay, I've completely hacked pwuid and gui lookups out of the loop and it's a lot faster.

Makefile
#
# Makefile
#

all: libs

#
# Make a shared Library
#
libs: getpwuid.c
        gcc -shared -Wl,-soname,libfuncs.so.1 -o libfuncs.so.1.0  getpwuid.c
        ln -s libfuncs.so.1.0 libfuncs.so.1
        ln -s libfuncs.so.1 libfuncs.so


getpwuid.c
/*
 Put all the functions you want to override here
*/
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <pwd.h>


struct passwd *getpwuid(uid_t uid)
{
    return 0;
}

struct group *getgrgid(gid_t gid)
{
    return 0;
}

build and use:
make
setenv LD_PRELOAD $PWD/libfuncs.so.1.0

messages.author: 37fbc81a6a87deab
messages.subject: Re: Performance, parallelism
parts:
The multicore::parallel seems to be working nice with Shiny, with additional advantage of giving live feedback from worker process.
A simple example of implementation:

1) Simulate expensive function:

f <- function(x) {
for(i in 1:3) {
multicore::sendMaster(as.character(i))
Sys.sleep(2)
}
sqrt(x)
}
2) Run in server:

values <- reactiveValues( res=NULL, calcMsg1 = NULL )
observe( {
if (is.null(proc)) {
proc <<- multicore::parallel(f( 10 ))) 
values$calcMsg1 <- 'Started'
invalidateLater(1000)
} else if ( multicore::selectChildren(proc) == multicore::processID(proc) ) {

values$res <- res
values$calcMsg1 <-  paste('FINISHED:',res) 
}
} else { invalidateLater(1000); }

proc = NULL was initially defied inside shinyServer function parameters, e.g. shinyServer(function(input, output, proc = NULL) { ...

1) Run multiple Shiny Server processes and/or machines and put them behind a load balancer. For multiple Shiny Server processes per machine, you'd need to have a config file per Shiny Server process and have each process listening on a different port.
2) Configure Shiny Server to launch multiple processes for a given app. This isn't currently possible but is on the plan for later this year.

How urgent is the bottleneck for you right now? Is the app unusable for you as deployed right now, or was it just right after your announcement?

On Wednesday, March 6, 2013 5:38:46 PM UTC-5, Alex wrote:
The multicore::parallel seems to be working nice with Shiny, with additional advantage of giving live feedback from worker process.
A simple example of implementation:

1) Simulate expensive function:

f <- function(x) {
for(i in 1:3) {
multicore::sendMaster(as.character(i))
Sys.sleep(2)
}
sqrt(x)
}
2) Run in server:

values <- reactiveValues( res=NULL, calcMsg1 = NULL )
observe( {
if (is.null(proc)) {
proc <<- multicore::parallel(f( 10 ))) 
values$calcMsg1 <- 'Started'
invalidateLater(1000)
} else if ( multicore::selectChildren(proc) == multicore::processID(proc) ) {
res <- multicore::collect(proc, wait=FALSE)[[1]]
if( class(res) == 'character' ) {
invalidateLater(1000)
values$calcMsg1 <- res
} else {
multicore::collect(proc)
proc <<- NULL
values$res <- res
values$calcMsg1 <-  paste('FINISHED:',res) 
}
} else { invalidateLater(1000); }
}, label='CalcMain', suspended = FALSE )

After execution we have final result in values$res. 
While execution we can send feedback to browser using values$calcMsg1.

Notes:

proc = NULL was initially defied inside shinyServer function parameters, e.g. shinyServer(function(input, output, proc = NULL) { ...
This allows different browser connections fork multiple workers, while only 1 worker is allowed per connection. I believe it can be also defined as reactive value.

Last multicore::collect(proc) is mainly to ensure that R cleaned-up after forking and we would not run into memory problems.

I advise to use multicore::children() to limit number of workers depending on number of cores and available memory.

The function assumes that message class is 'character' and final result class is NOT 'character'. This can be easily fixed by defining and returning e.g. "message" class object.

Joe, you are right that this would not work for all apps, but in case of app with one/few expensive function(s) (e.g. calculating on big datasets) and many light functions (e.g plotting) it seems to work OK.
.
